sections.heading: Cantilever driving low frequency piezoelectric energy harvester using single crystal material 0.71Pb(Mg1/3Nb2/3)O3-0.29PbTiO3
sections.text:
Chundong Xu,1,2, BoRen,1Wening Di,hu Liang,1 Jie Jiao, Lingying Li,1,   
LongLi,1 2 Xiangyong Zhao,1 Haosu Luo,1 and Dong Wang1   
Key Laboratory of Inorganic Functional Material and Device, Shanghai Institute ofCeramics,   
Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai 201800, China   
2Graduate School of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China

(Received 17 May 2012; accepted 28 June 2012; published online 16 July 2012)

We present a high performance piezoelectric energy harvester CANtilever Driving Low frequency Energy harvester (CANDLE) consisting of cantilever beam and cymbal transducers based on piezoelectric single crystal $0 . 7 1 \mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { M g } _ { 1 / 3 } \mathrm { N b } _ { 2 / 3 } ) \mathrm { O } _ { 3 } { - } 0 . 2 9 \mathrm { P b } \mathrm { T i O } _ { 3 }$ Electrical properties of CANDLE under different proof masses, excitation frequencies, and load resistances are studied systematically. Under an acceleration of $3 . 2 g$ $( g = 9 . 8 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 } )$ , a peak voltage of $3 8 \mathrm { V }$ , a maximum power of $3 . 7 ~ \mathrm { \ m W }$ were measured at $1 0 2 \mathrm { H z }$ with a proof mass of $4 . 2 \mathrm { g }$ . Low resonance frequency and high power output performance demonstrate the promise of the device in energy harvesting for wireless sensors and low-power electronics. $©$ 2012 American Institute of Physics. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1063/1.4737170]

Energy harvesting technologies basing on piezoelectric properties have drawn considerable attentions during last o deces.zecti nyhst s e energy density, better electromechanical coupling and easy integration with micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS), and integrated circuit (IC) technologies, comparing with electrostatic and electromagnetic vibration energy harvesters. Unique merits make it promising for self-power devices, such as wireless sensor dots, autonomous energy-scavenging sensors, and other low power electronics with the applications ranging from biomedicine to homeland security. .4.5

In the previous studies, lead zirconate titanate (PZT) ceramics, piezoelectric polymer polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) and copolymers, piezoelectric composites materials, and ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires were commonly applied on piezoelectric energy harvesting. Recently, relaxor piezoelectric single crystal material $( 1 - x ) \mathrm { P b } (  { \mathbf { M } }  { \mathbf { g } } _ { 1 / 3 }  { \mathbf { N } }  { \mathbf { b } } _ { 2 / 3 } )  { \mathbf { O } } _ { 3 ^ { - } } x  { \mathbf { P } }  { \mathbf { b } }  { \mathrm { T i O } } _ { 3 }$ (PMN-$x \mathrm { P T }$ or PMNT) has attracted continuous attention for designing and fabricating high-efficiency piezoelectric transducers, due to its well-known ultrahigh electromechanical response $\left( d _ { 3 3 } \right.$ and $k _ { 3 3 }$ could reach as high as $2 5 0 0 ~ \mathrm { p C / N }$ and 0.94, respectively) and energy density (d33.833 \~78 000 × 1015 $\mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } / \mathrm { N } )$ .6 9 However, applications of the material in piezoelectric energy harvesting have not attracted sufficient attentions. Usually, excitation frequencies of ambient vibration sources are normally below $3 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ according to previous statistics.10Unfortunately, maximum powers obtained at resonance frequencies below $3 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ would be problematic for micro-scale vibration energy harvesters. Cantilever configuration consisting of a piezoelectric beam and a proof mass is a reasonable choice to lower resonance frequency for piezoelectric energy harvesters.11 However, mechanical stress in piezoelectric materials along the cantilever beam is nonuniform during bending vibration. Stress gradually increases from the base to the tip of cantilever beam along the length direction, which limits the conversion efficiency of piezoelectric materials nearby the tip of the cantilever beam in vibration energy harvesting. In 1991, Newnham presented a high performance piezoelectric transducer named cymbal.12Kim introduced this structure into energy harvesting in 2004.13 Cymbal energy harvesters mainly work in the $k _ { 3 1 }$ excitation mode for rectangle piezoelectric transducers. Mechanical stress generated in piezoelectric materials is not only uniformly distributed but also amplified by this special configuration, so the energy conversion capacity of piezoelectric materials can be fully developed.i4 Nevertheless, high resonance frequency is a main drawback for cymbal, and it is a big challenge to lower the resonance frequency below $3 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ .

Combining traditional cantilever beam with cymbal transducer is an effective way to improve the properties of piezoelectric energy harvester. In this letter, we introduce an energy harvester named CANtilever Driving Low frequency Energy harvester (CANDLE), which consists of one cantilever beam, two PMNT-stainless steel cymbals, and an aluminum alloy frame, as shown in Fig. 1(a). With this special structure, CANDLE not only lowers resonance frequency of cymbal transducers dramatically but also increases output power immensely compared with previous results.15 CANDLE can also be constituted by cantilever beam and other piezoelectric transducers besides cymbal, such as Moonie, Thunder, and multilayer transducers. Compositing different energy harvesting structures basing on their own advantages has rarely been tried by other scientists so far.

The typical CANDLE composite structure is showed in Fig. 1(a). A high-quality 0.71PMN-0.29PT single crystal ingot was grown directly from the melt by a modified Bridgman technique, then diced into $\langle 0 0 1 \rangle$ oriented plates with dimensions of $2 5 \mathrm { m m }$ length, $5 \mathrm { m m }$ width, and $1 \mathrm { m m }$ thickness. The silver electrodes were painted on the plates and fired at $7 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for $3 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ . Then, the as-prepared plates were poled in silicon oil along their thickness directions under an electric voltage of $1 \mathrm { k V }$ for $1 5 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ at $1 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ with half of the voltage in the cooling run. The $d _ { 3 1 }$ piezoelectric coefficient of the polarized PMNT crystal plates was measured to be $- 6 5 0 \mathrm { ~ \ p C / N }$ by an Agilent $4 2 9 4 \mathrm { A }$ impedance analyzer di    nd o pa sandwiched between two protruded rectangular stainless steel (SUS 304) caps along the thickness directions using silver-loaded epoxy (Applied Products E-Solder 3021) to form the cymbal-type piezoelectric PMNT single crystalstainless steel transducer. A normal cantilever beam was fabricated by a beryllium copper (C17200) slice with dimensions of $3 5 \mathrm { m m }$ length, $5 \mathrm { m m }$ width, and $0 . 5 \mathrm { { m m } }$ thickness. The two protruded rectangular stainless steel caps, each of $2 5 \mathrm { m m }$ total length $( l _ { c } )$ , $2 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ top-flange length $( l _ { t } )$ , and $1 1 \mathrm { m m }$ bottom-flange length $( l _ { b } )$ , were made by diepunching a stainless steel sheet with thickness of $0 . 3 \mathrm { m m }$ and the same width as the PMNT plates. One cantilever beam and two PMNT-stainless steel cymbal transducers were assembled and clamped by an aluminium alloy frame to form a composite structure piezoelectric energy harvester-CANDLE, as shown in Fig. 1(a). Some insulated plastics were filled between the cymbals, cantilever, and aluminium alloy frame to prevent electrical connection.

![](images/fe3dbf817207e0546419b01c2ef2c5f19532d100c27e4e485cd6d8d66f587c94.jpg)  
FIG. 1. (a) The schematic diagram of CANDLE and (b) SDOF model of vibration energy harvesters.

The working principle of the device can be stated as follows. First, a mechanical vibration is applied on the base of the device along the transverse direction (Fig. 1(a)). With the base vibrating, the cantilever beam clamped by the two PMNT-stainless steel cymbals will produce mechanical stress because of transverse oscillating. The mechanical stress is then transferred to the PMNT-stainless steel cymbals squeezed by the beryllium copper cantilever beam and aluminium alloy frame. After amplified by the cymbal transducers, stress is delivered to the high performance PMNT piezoelectric single crystal to convert mechanical stress into electrical energy. Here, working frequency of the PMNTstainless steel cymbal is lowered by resonance of cantilever beam. On the other hand, stress applied on the PMNT single crystal is amplified by cymbal structures and cantilever beam, respectively. Amplifying capability of the cymbal transducers has been studied systematically by former researchers.11 To demonstrate the stress amplified capability of CANDLE, the forces applied on energy harvesters of cymbal and CANDLE through proof mass are compared according to single degree of freedom (SDOF) energy harvesting theoretical model. Fig. 1(b) is the SDOF model of piezoelectric energy harvesting. $m _ { e q } , b _ { e q } ,$ and $k _ { e q }$ are equivalent mass, equivalent mechanical damping coefficient, and equivalent stiffness, respectively. The displacement of the proof mass relative to the base according to SDOF model can be expressed as1 19

$$
z ( t ) = \frac { \left( \frac { \omega } { \omega _ { n } } \right) ^ { 2 } } { \sqrt { [ 1 - ( \frac { \omega } { \omega _ { n } } ) ^ { 2 } ] ^ { 2 } + ( 2 \zeta \frac { \omega } { \omega _ { n } } ) ^ { 2 } } } Y \mathrm { s i n } ( \omega t - \phi ) .
$$

Here, $z = x - y$ , and $Y$ is displacement amplitude of the base. $\omega _ { n }$ and $\omega$ are eigenfrequency of the device and vibration excitation frequency, respectively. $\zeta$ and $\phi$ are the mechanical damping factor and initial phase angle.

Through Eq. (1), excitation forces generated by proof masses can be expressed as

$$
F ( t ) = m \ddot { z } ( t ) = - \frac { m ( \frac { \omega } { \omega _ { n } } ) ^ { 2 } \omega ^ { 2 } } { \sqrt { \left[ 1 - \left( \frac { \omega } { \omega _ { n } } \right) ^ { 2 } \right] ^ { 2 } + \left( 2 \zeta \frac { \omega } { \omega _ { n } } \right) ^ { 2 } } } Y \mathrm { s i n } ( \omega t - \phi ) .
$$

Here, $\ddot { z } ( t )$ is acceleration of the proof mass. The amplified capability of CANDLE can be demonstrated by the forces ratio of $\boldsymbol { F } _ { c y }$ and $F _ { c a }$ that generate by proof masses of cymbal and CANDLE, respectively. With the same base vibration and proof mass, $F _ { c y } / F _ { c a }$ can be expressed as

$$
\frac { F _ { c y } } { F _ { c a } } = \frac { ( \frac { \omega _ { n 2 } } { \omega _ { n 1 } } ) ^ { 2 } \sqrt { [ 1 - ( \frac { \omega } { \omega _ { n 2 } } ) ^ { 2 } ] ^ { 2 } + ( 2 \zeta \frac { \omega } { \omega _ { n 2 } } ) ^ { 2 } } } { \sqrt { [ 1 - ( \frac { \omega } { \omega _ { n 1 } } ) ^ { 2 } ] ^ { 2 } + ( { 2 \zeta \frac { \omega } { \omega _ { n 1 } } } ) ^ { 2 } } } .
$$

$\omega _ { n 1 }$ and $\omega _ { n 2 }$ are eigenfrequencies of cymbal and CANDLE. It is assumed that $\omega _ { n 1 } / \omega _ { n 2 } = 1 0$ and $\zeta = 0 . 0 5$ Fig. 2 is the force ratio diagram of $F _ { c y } / F _ { c a }$ . It can be found that the forces generated by proof masses of cymbal and CANDLE are approximately equivalent at higher excitation frequency when $\omega / \omega _ { n 1 } \geq 1$ (above the resonance frequency of the cymbal energy harvester). However, when the base excitation is below the resonance frequency of the cymbal, excitation force applied on CANDLE by proof mass increases promptly comparing with cymbal energy harvester. The phenomenon can be observed from Fig. 2 when $F _ { c y } / F _ { c a }$ drops speedily below 1.0 when $\omega / \omega _ { n 1 } < 1$ .The inset of Fig. 2 is an enlarged scale of the red circle part, which implies that $F _ { c y } / F _ { c a }$ reaches a minimum of 0.001 when $\omega / \omega _ { n 1 } = 0 . 1$ (corresponds to the resonance frequency of CANDLE). At this time, $F _ { c a }$ is approximately 1000 times larger than $F _ { c y }$ .

![](images/f0dbb15104b6a59268a3bb02431663bc020fc395590d111c7ed64eea100bab9c.jpg)  
FIG. 2. Frequency dependence of forces ratio $( F _ { c y } / F _ { c a } )$ of the CANDLE and cymbal energy harvesters with the same vibration excitation and proof mass. The inset shows the enlarged scale of the red circle part in the lower excitation frequency.

The analysis results demonstrate that the cantilever beam amplify the force applying on cymbal transducer, and CANDLE can generate much more energy than cymbal energy harvester at lower excitation frequency. So CANDLE could be a high performance low resonance frequency piezoelectric energy harvester driven by cantilever beam comparing with the traditional piezoelectric energy harvesters.

The experiment setup is presented as follows. A mechanical Shaker (Brüel & Kjær Ltd., Type 4809) which can supply a maximum force of $4 5 \mathrm { N }$ $( 1 0 \mathrm { H z } { - } 2 0 \mathrm { k H z } )$ was used to excite the device, and the shaker was put on a spongy cushion to relieve any interference from the surroundings. The base of the device was fixed to the shaker with screws, and the shaker was driven by an arbitrary function generator (Agilent 33220A) and power amplifier (Brüel & Kjær Ltd., Type 2706) to supply a sinusoidal excitation of the desired magnitude and frequency. Acceleration generated by the shaker can be monitored by charge accelerometer (Brüel & Kjær Ltd., Type 4374) and charge amplifier (Brüel & Kjær Ltd., Type 2635). The output voltage from the device was monitored by a Tektronix Digital Oscilloscope (Agilent 54622A). For the open-circuit, an impedance matching circuit which can avoid impedance interference of the device was design using a chip TL084CN (ST microelectronics). During our experiments, various load resistances were used in order to characterize the performances of the device. The power under different load resistances $R _ { L }$ was calculated using the formula $P = U ^ { 2 } / R _ { L }$ , where $U$ is the output peak voltage. All the measurements were performed at room temperature and ambient pressure.

The experimental results obtained from the characterization of CANDLE for energy harvesting purposes are presented and discussed. Fig. 3 is the frequency response functions (FRFs) of open-circuit voltage and generated power of the device with different proof masses. Here, the generated power is calculated by the formula $P = 1 / 2 C _ { 0 } U _ { o p e n } ^ { 2 } f$ Open-circuit voltage $U _ { o p e n }$ is monitored through an impedance matching circuit which can avoid impedance interference of the device. $C _ { 0 }$ and $f$ are the static capacitance of the device and vibration frequency of mechanical excitation. Acceleration generated by the shaker changes nonlinearly with the increasing of excitation frequency, so open-circuit voltage and generated power are normalized divided by the acceleration and the square of the acceleration according to the SDOF piezoelectric energy harvesting theoretical model.20 Normalized open-circuit voltage and generated power can fully characterize the properties of the device regardless of different ambient vibration sources.21 Fig. 3 shows that increasing of the proof mass not only enables the device to convert more electrical energy from vibration sources but also lowers the resonance frequency of the device. Resonance frequency $f _ { r }$ is merely $5 5 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ even for proof mass equals to zero and is much lower than that of the previously reported cymbal energy harvester.15 The maximum normalized open-circuit voltage and generated power are $1 . 7 5 ~ \mathrm { V s } ^ { 2 } / \mathrm { m }$ and $7 . 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 7 } \ \mathrm { { W s ^ { 4 } / m ^ { 2 } } }$ with $4 . 2 \mathrm { g }$ proof mass, respectively.

Fig. 4 shows the outputs of the device with a $4 . 2 \mathrm { g }$ proof mass as a function of the load resistances under resonant excitation. The experiments were carried out with an acceleration of $3 . 2 g$ $\mathrm { \bar { ( } g = 9 . 8 m / s ^ { 2 } }$ supplied by the Shaker. A maximum output power of $3 . 7 \mathrm { m W }$ can be obtained from the device at $1 0 2 \mathrm { H z }$ with a matching load resistance of $2 5 1 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , and the peak voltage reaches $3 8 \mathrm { V }$ under the same vibration condition. The power density reaches $2 9 . 6 \mathrm { \ m W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ . The maximum output voltage and generated power are 5 and 4.8 times of previously reported results of the cymbal energy harvester. The resonance frequency of $1 0 2 \mathrm { H z }$ is much lower than that of the cymbal energy harvester with $4 . 2 \mathrm { g }$ proof mass (above $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ It   p cation of CANDLE in energy harvesting.

FIG. 4. Load resistance dependence of the output voltage and electrical power of the device with proof mass of $4 . 2 \mathrm { g }$ under excitation acceleration of $3 . 2 g$ at the resonance frequency of $1 0 2 \mathrm { H z }$ .

The output voltage and power of the device with different proof masses under the excitation acceleration of $3 . 2 g$ are also studied, as shown in Fig. 5. Three conclusions can be summarized from the experimental results. First, maximum voltage and power of the device increase dramatically with the proof mass. This property is similar to the cantilever energy harvester. Second, matching load resistances for maximum output power also increase with the proof mass in Fig. 5(b). Because larger proof mass indicates lower resonance frequency of the device, and matching load resistance can be approximately expressed by $Z = 1 / \omega C _ { 0 }$ . Third, the increasing of output power ceases when proof mass increases to a large enough value. This phenomenon may be caused by that the fringe of the PMNT-stainless steel cymbal transducers and aluminum alloy frame confine transverse displacement of the cantilever beam when vibration acceleration or proof mass is large enough. This property gives selfprotection capability of the special structure that could avoid the stress in the piezoelectric materials exceeding its endurance. Experimental results illustrate that a maximum power of $4 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m W }$ is obtained for the CANDLE device with a $2 . 1 \mathrm { g }$ proof mass, which is 8 times larger than previously reported results and demonstrates its high performance in vibration energy harvesting. Compared with the traditional cymbal device, the resonance frequency of CANDLE is only $1 0 2 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ with $4 . 2 \mathrm { g }$ proof mass, while the maximum power output is much higher $3 . 7 \mathrm { m W }$ at $1 0 2 \mathrm { H z }$ to $0 . 7 7 \mathrm { m W }$ above $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ ).

![](images/83f2ca0c3433281f55208863527d90deb32d0e851df4eb340bd4a3d872778306.jpg)  
FIG. 5. Load resistance dependence of the output voltage (a) and electrical power (b) of the device with different proof masses under excitation of acceleration $3 . 2 g$ at the resonance frequency.

In summary, a vibration energy harvester CANDLE constituted by cantilever beam and cymbal transducers basing on high performance piezoelectric single crystal $0 . 7 1 \mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { M g } _ { 1 / 3 } \mathrm { N b } _ { 2 / 3 } ) \mathrm { O } _ { 3 } { - } 0 . 2 9 \mathrm { P b } \mathrm { T i O } _ { 3 }$ has been designed and fabricated. A method to study energy harvesting by compositing different piezoelectric transducer structures to enhance the properties of energy harvesting is introduced. Force amplifying capability of CANDLE is illustrated, and the electrical properties under different proof masses, frequencies and load resistances are studied systematically. Experiment results show that CANDLE using PMNT single crystal material can lower resonance frequency and increase output power dramatically. Under the acceleration excitation of $3 . 2 g$ , the device with $4 . 2 \mathrm { g }$ proof mass can generate a peak voltage of $3 8 \mathrm { V }$ and a maximum power of $3 . 7 \mathrm { m W }$ at $1 0 2 \mathrm { H z }$ with a matching load resistance of $2 5 1 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ .
